meta.regime: A genuine risk-off session arrived - the Nvidia fallout ran into a second week, the Nikkei fell 1.6% to 60,182.50, the Kospi 2.8% and MSCI's Asia gauge 1.9% - and the haven bid went to the yen alone. Gold at 3,852.59 is down 0.75%, silver at 47.47 down 2.56% to a yearly low and copper at 6.00 down 1.23% to a four-month low, all falling alongside equities because a December Fed hike now priced at 92% to 93.5% outranks the haven trade, while Japan's Q3 GDP came in flat at 0.0% quarter on quarter against a 0.1% forecast and the yen strengthened against every other currency on this board regardless.

nextEvent.why: Tomorrow at 15:30, the first genuine two-way US data risk since the October CPI print on November 10, and the test of whether the consumer can carry a December Fed path the whole board is positioned long.
nextEvent.priced: December 9 Fed hike about 92% to 93.5%, with a 6.5% to 8% tail for fifty basis points

scenarios.then: The first real crack in a 92% path - sell DXY, cover the USD/CAD long and buy gold.
Path intact, the dollar holds plus two and USD/CAD extends toward 1.4350.
December is sealed and the fifty-point tail grows - sell gold and press USD/CAD; USD/JPY stays capped at 160.

meta.nextBigEvent: US October retail sales Tuesday 15:30 - headline forecast plus 0.2% from plus 0.8%, the first two-way test of a Fed path priced near 92%.

update.title: 🇦🇺 AUD analysis updated
update.text: Bullock kept inflation risks skewed to the upside and flagged high oil, declining to confirm the priced peak. AUD/USD still fell to 0.67318, minus 0.58%. Minutes 02:30.

dailyRead: The weekend's diagnosis survived contact with a live session, but one leg of it broke, and that is where this report should start. Last week's argument for being short the franc rested on a specific claim: that a genuine equity scare had arrived, the franc had not been bid in it, and the dollar had taken the haven trade outright. This morning delivered a second, larger scare - the Nvidia fallout ran into a new week, the Nikkei fell 1.6% to 60,182.50, the Kospi 2.8% to 5,142.84, Advantest dropped about 10.4%, Lasertec 10.7% and Tokyo Electron 5.7% - and the franc firmed against everything except the yen: USD/CHF 0.83840 and minus 0.06%, EUR/CHF 0.92406 and minus 0.08%, GBP/CHF 1.10742 and minus 0.10%, AUD/CHF 0.56609 and minus 0.35%. The dollar, meanwhile, did not take the bid at all - DXY is 103.396 and minus 0.02%. So the franc moves from minus one to zero and every franc short on this board loses a conviction notch. That is a leg breaking, said plainly, and not a reversal: one firm session does not undo a 5.33% annual loss against the dollar, and TradingEconomics itself frames the move as carry-unwinding into a renewed haven bid rather than anything the Swiss National Bank has done. The second and larger story is Japan, and it is genuinely odd. Preliminary Q3 GDP landed at 01:50 flat at 0.0% quarter on quarter against a 0.1% consensus, contracting 0.1% annualised against a plus 0.3% forecast - the first fall in four quarters. Net trade took 0.6 percentage points off growth, more than the 0.4 expected, and private consumption, over half the economy, fell 0.3%; business investment rose 1.6%. A contraction ought to be the thing that kills a December hike, and the yen strengthened against all seven of the others anyway: USD/JPY 159.406 and minus 0.19%, EUR/JPY 175.685 minus 0.20%, GBP/JPY 210.559 minus 0.22%, AUD/JPY 107.622 minus 0.48%, CHF/JPY 190.114 minus 0.12%. Two reasons, and both matter for the next four to six weeks. The intervention line at 160 is now close enough that traders are positioning around the Ministry of Finance rather than around the Bank of Japan - the Ministry spent a record 15.4 trillion yen defending it between July 30 and August 3. And the AI rout is doing what 400 basis points of carry had prevented: forcing an unwind of yen-funded positions. TradingEconomics still carries a 1.5% forecast for the December 18 meeting, and the economist read is that weak consumption is itself a symptom of high prices and therefore an argument for tightening, not against it. So the yen moves from zero to plus one - the first time this file has had it above neutral in weeks - with the honest caveat that the upgrade is leaning on an equity rout, and Tuesday's Nvidia print is its single clearest invalidation. The third thing is a correction of emphasis on the metals, and it is the cleanest confirmation on the board. In a true risk-off session gold, silver and copper all fell: gold 3,852.59 and minus 0.75%, down 6.96% on the month and at its lowest since October 2025; silver 47.47 and minus 2.56%, minus 16.83% on the month and at a one-year low; copper 6.00 and minus 1.23%, minus 8.16% on the month and a four-month low. Metals that fall when equities fall are not trading the haven axis, they are trading US real rates, and the 10-year TIPS yield at 2.90% with the 10-year nominal at 5.15% and the 2-year at 4.87% says which. The Fed path is why: CME-based pricing for December 9 has moved to roughly 92% to 93.5% for a quarter-point, from 88.8% on November 10 and about 72% a week before that, and a hike takes the range to 4.00% to 4.25%. One correction to Friday's file is owed here. It said the half-point had no trigger left because Waller's stated condition had passed; the reporting is that his condition was October core at 0.3% or more, October core printed 0.3%, and the market still carries a 6.5% to 8% tail for fifty basis points. That tail is small, but it is not zero, and this file should not have called it dead. Copper deserves its own caveat, because the short is more crowded than it is clean: the selling is paper and macro - Goldman attributes it largely to AI equity volatility - while the physical market is tight, with Shanghai warehouse stocks at 27,642 tonnes, the lowest since late December, and the Yangshan import premium at a record 285 dollars a tonne on Friday. Fourth, the Aussie, which is now unambiguously the worst currency on this board and goes to minus two. AUD/USD is 0.67510 and minus 0.30%, a fresh low beneath Friday's 0.6771, and it is the weakest major against every single counterpart: minus 0.48% against the yen, minus 0.35% against the franc, minus 0.26% against the Canadian dollar, minus 0.21% against the kiwi. The policy diagnosis from the weekend is intact - the Reserve Bank raised to 4.85% on November 3, a five-hike year and the highest since late 2008, but removed the explicit reference to further increases, three of nine voted to hold, and Bullock said plainly that she does not know what the next move will be - and copper at a four-month low is now compounding rather than causing it. Governor Bullock speaks tonight at 00:50 and the minutes follow at 02:30, which is where this thesis gets confirmed or broken; Thursday's October employment at 02:30, forecast plus 25,200 after minus 39,329, is the genuine two-way risk on a very crowded short. Fifth, the day's actual event, which is Canadian. October CPI lands at 15:30 with m/m forecast plus 0.3% from plus 0.1% and the median and trimmed cores at 2.0% and 1.9%, and it is the last inflation reading before December 9. RBC expects headline to ease to about 3.0% from 3.1% with core slipping to 1.9%, and calls a hike its low-conviction base case; Wells Fargo flags upside risk from October oil; the market prices the meeting at roughly a coin flip, about 54% as of Saturday. Set against that: unemployment at a six-month high of 6.7%, a third consecutive monthly fall in employment, and WTI at 88.76 which is up 0.23% today but down 9.92% on the month. The Canadian dollar stays at zero precisely because the evidence cancels, and this print is what breaks the tie. Finally the two that did not move and the one nuance worth flagging. Sterling at 1.32101 and the euro at 1.10218 are both flat and both stay at plus one, with Wednesday's UK CPI at 09:00 - forecast 3.6% from 3.5%, core steady at 2.8% - the week's binary for the pound, followed by Bailey at 09:30 and again at 17:00. The euro's nuance is new and cuts against Friday's framing: this file has been treating the December 17 hike to 2.75% as a fully owned endpoint because all 71 economists in the Reuters poll expect it and 46 of them call it the peak. But the market is more hawkish than the economists - ECB Watch had December at about 92% on November 13 and Bloomberg reports traders pricing three more moves over the next year, while 25 of those 71 economists do see another in early 2027. A priced endpoint is still worth less than an unpriced path, so sterling stays ahead of the euro, but the gap is narrower than Friday's file implied and EUR/GBP is correctly a range rather than a view.

today.headline: Bullock refused to confirm the priced pause at 00:50 - inflation risks still skewed to the upside, oil flagged - and the Aussie fell anyway to 0.67318, minus 0.58%.
today.read: The words were the mild hawkish push back this file named as the invalidation, but price ignored them: a fresh low, the weakest since late January, against a board whose own guidance still has unemployment rising more than anticipated. The verdict stays at minus two because the data has not changed, and the thesis now has one honest hole in it - the governor is not endorsing the market's peak. The minutes at 02:30 and what the three dissenters argued are the next test, then jobs Thursday 02:30 against plus 25,200 on a very crowded short.

today.headline: Warsh's 19:00 remarks in San Francisco said nothing on rates or inflation, and DXY drifted to 103.52, plus 0.11%, with the 10-year flat at 5.14%.
today.read: A non-event for the path, which is itself the information: the chair passed up the chance to lean against a December hike priced around 92% to 93.5% on Friday's reading - a post-speech CME figure is not yet verifiable. The one thing to keep is his bust scenario, where AI returns turn down and stocks fall, because that is the rout already running. Tuesday's retail sales at 15:30 and Wednesday's minutes at 21:00 are the real tests.

today.headline: October CPI missed: m/m plus 0.2% against plus 0.3%, trimmed 1.8% against 1.9%, median 2.0% in line, and headline y/y held 3.1% where 3.2% was expected.
today.read: The one number that was supposed to decide December 9 came in soft on two of its three red-folder lines, and the Canadian dollar fell against every other currency on this board inside the hour - USD/CAD 1.42946 and plus 0.18%, from 1.42734 and plus 0.03% before the print. Score to minus one and the meeting now reads hold rather than a coin flip. The next inputs are Gravelle on Wednesday at 19:30 and crude, which is down another 1.00% today at 87.68.

today.read: Net trade took 0.6 points off growth and consumption fell 0.3%, yet TradingEconomics still forecasts 1.50% on December 18 and the economists read weak consumption as a symptom of high prices rather than a reason to stop. The real change is the carry unwind the AI rout is forcing, which is the one thing that has ever beaten a 400 basis point differential. Score to plus one, with Tuesday's Nvidia print the clearest invalidation.

TradingEconomics frames it as the franc's renewed haven status eroding carry returns and forcing an unwind, not as anything the SNB did - its language has in fact softened since September. Score from minus one to zero: franc shorts are downgraded a notch, not reversed, with 0.00% policy still the anchor.

today.headline: Quiet at 0.55213 and minus 0.07%, holding up better than the Aussie for the fourth session running.
today.read: AUD/NZD at 1.22282 and minus 0.21% keeps grinding lower and remains the highest-conviction cross on the board. Tuesday's Q4 inflation expectations at 04:00, previous 2.34%, is the cleanest single read on December 9, where TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% while ANZ expects a pause - a real forecaster split. The Financial Stability Report lands tonight at 22:00.

today.read: All 71 Reuters economists expect the move, but only 46 call it the peak, and the market is the more hawkish side - about 92% on ECB Watch for December and traders priced for three more moves over the next year. That narrows the gap to sterling without closing it. Headline HICP at 4.0% against core at 2.5% still says the hike is bought with energy; Lagarde speaks Wednesday 16:25.

today.headline: Flat at 1.32101 and minus 0.02%, waiting on Wednesday, which is the week's binary for the pound.

December 17 is the only December outside the US that is not effectively priced, which is the whole reason sterling stays at the top of the non-dollar group.

snapshot.t: Bullock would not confirm the pause the market has priced, and the Aussie fell through her anyway
snapshot.s: On the ASIC Annual Forum panel at 00:50 she kept the board's view that inflation risks are still skewed to the upside and flagged the risk of oil staying high - a push back on pricing that had written December off, with no new guidance reported and no transcript published. snapshot.t: Hormuz escalated over the weekend and crude still will not bid - the premium has stopped being paid
snapshot.s: Iran said it targeted a US radar in Bahrain, the Revolutionary Guards claimed tankers struck mines and said the strait remains closed, and the US military disputes the mine claims. WTI is 88.76 and plus 0.23%, Brent 95.75 and minus 0.10% and down 12.60% on the month. A decaying premium bleeds; an escalation gaps. USOIL stays a range.

USD.when: December 9 at 21:00, with new projections, and the live question remains the path rather than the size
USD.note: TradingEconomics carries the Fed funds rate at 4.00% for October as the upper bound of the 3.75% to 4.00% range, held on October 28 with Cook and Hammack dissenting for a quarter-point rise. December pricing has firmed again rather than stalled: CME-based measures are roughly 92% to 93.5% for a quarter-point, from 88.8% on November 10 and about 72% a week before, which would take the range to 4.00% to 4.25%. One correction to Friday's file: it called the half-point dead because Waller's condition had passed, but his stated condition was October core at 0.3% or more, October core printed 0.3%, and the market still carries a 6.5% to 8% tail for fifty basis points. Wednesday's October 28 minutes at 21:00 are the week's real Fed event and will show how wide the hawkish bloc is. Warsh's 19:00 opening remarks in San Francisco confirmed that he gave no December signal: the text on federalreserve.gov never mentions interest rates or inflation and says only that the technology has important implications for monetary policy down the road. That leaves the path exactly where pricing had it.

EUR.when: December 17 at 15:15, the final meeting of 2026 and, on the economists' consensus, the final hike of the cycle
EUR.note: The deposit facility rate is 2.50% on TradingEconomics - the main refinancing rate is 2.65% and is not the policy rate for this board - after an October 29 hold. All 71 economists in the Reuters poll taken November 10 to 12 expect 2.75% on December 17, but the split inside that poll is the part this file under-weighted: 46 see 2.75% as the peak and 25 see another move in early 2027. The market is the more hawkish of the two, with ECB Watch at about 92% for December on November 13 and Bloomberg reporting traders priced for three more moves over the next year. That narrows the gap to sterling rather than closing it, because a priced endpoint is still worth less than an unpriced path. Headline HICP is 4.0%, a three-year high, against core steady at 2.5%, so the hike is still being bought with energy: EU gas is 90.14 euros and up 186.92% on the year. Lagarde speaks Wednesday 16:25, Thursday 15:30 and Friday 10:15.

GBP.when: December 17 at 14:00, still genuinely live, with Wednesday's CPI at 09:00 the thing that moves it
GBP.note: Bank Rate is 4.00% after the November 5 increase, voted 8-1 with Catherine Mann dissenting for a half-point to 4.25% - the first rise since August 2023. The Bank projects CPI rising to around 5% by the middle of next year from 3.5% before energy effects fade, and said activity data have generally been stronger than expected. Bailey has signalled another increase may be needed unless inflation risks ease while warning against reading November as the start of a long series, and Lombardelli has kept December open without committing. Wednesday is the week's binary for sterling: October CPI at 09:00 is forecast 3.6% from 3.5% with core steady at 2.8% and RPI 4.1%, Bailey speaks at 09:30 and again at 17:00, and Tuesday's labour data at 09:00 leans the same way with average earnings forecast to slow to 3.5% from 3.7%.

JPY.when: December 18 at 05:00, which survived a contracting quarter, with intervention the nearer event risk
JPY.note: The policy rate is 1.25% after an 8-1 October hold, with Hajime Takata dissenting for a faster move toward neutral, following consecutive quarter-point hikes in June and September that took borrowing costs to their highest since April 1995. The test came at 01:50 and the hike passed it: Q3 GDP was flat at 0.0% quarter on quarter against a 0.1% forecast and minus 0.1% annualised, and TradingEconomics still carries 1.50% as its December 18 forecast, with a Reuters-poll majority and an 83% Bloomberg survey reading pointing the same way. The economists' argument is that consumption falling 0.3% is itself a symptom of high prices and so supports tightening. What has actually changed is the other side: the AI rout is forcing an unwind of yen-funded carry, which is the one thing that has ever beaten 400 basis points of rate differential, and the Ministry of Finance line at 160 - defended with a record 15.4 trillion yen between July 30 and August 3 - caps the alternative. National core CPI lands Friday 01:30, forecast 2.3% from 2.1%.

AUD.when: December 8 at 05:30, still the base case, but Bullock has now declined to endorse it and the minutes at 02:30 are the live test
AUD.note: The cash rate is 4.85% on TradingEconomics after the November 3 increase from 4.60%, carried 6-3 with three members voting to hold - the fifth hike of the year and the highest since late 2008. Bullock gave the first of this week's three domestic tests at 00:50, on the ASIC Annual Forum State of the Economy panel in Sydney, and she did not take the pause the market had already written in: wires report her saying the board's current view is that inflation risks are still skewed to the upside, and flagging the risk of oil prices remaining high. That is a push back rather than a signal - no new guidance on December was reported, and the RBA has published no transcript, its speeches page still carrying only the live broadcast. The dovish case therefore still rests on the board's own November guidance, which has inflation reaching the top of the 2 to 3 per cent band only in late 2027 while housing prices fall significantly and unemployment rises more than previously anticipated, and on the data: September employment minus 39,329, weak housing and falling consumer and business confidence. Price agreed with the data, not the governor - AUD/USD fell on through the remarks to 0.67318, minus 0.58%, the weakest since late January. TradingEconomics has the market implying an 82% probability that rates have peaked. The November minutes at 02:30 are next and carry what the three dissenters argued, the Q3 wage price index lands Wednesday 02:30 forecast plus 0.9%, and October employment Thursday 02:30 forecast plus 25,200.

NZD.when: December 9 at 03:00, a full Monetary Policy Statement, with Tuesday's inflation expectations at 04:00 the direct input
NZD.note: The official cash rate is 2.75% after October's hold, taken 4-3 against market pricing that had been near 90% for a hike - a genuine surprise. The committee said tighter policy is likely to be required, depending on the outlook, and flagged near-term inflation uncertainty from volatile oil and fuel prices. TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% for December 9; Westpac looks for December and February moves taking the rate to a 3.5% neutral, while ANZ has pencilled in a December pause, so the forecaster split is real. Headline CPI is 3.7% and falling, having undershot the bank's own 3.9% forecast, but its published track has inflation worsening to about 4.4% in Q4 - a central bank forecasting its own inflation higher before it improves. Tuesday's Q4 inflation expectations at 04:00, previous 2.34%, is a red folder and the cleanest read on December; the Financial Stability Report lands tonight 22:00 and Governor Breman speaks Wednesday 20:00.

CAD.when: December 9 at 16:45, a regular decision with no Monetary Policy Report, and today's CPI has taken it off the coin flip
CAD.note: The overnight rate is 2.50% after October's quarter-point increase, the first rise in three years. October CPI did not deliver the acceleration the hike case needed: m/m plus 0.2% against plus 0.3% forecast, trimmed 1.8% against 1.9%, median 2.0% in line, and headline y/y held at 3.1% where a Reuters poll looked for 3.2%. TradingEconomics also has core inflation down to 2.0% from 2.2%. The two preferred cores now average 1.9%, below the 2% midpoint, which is not the persistence the bank described in October when it called inflation higher and more persistent than in the July Report and put CPI at an average 3% in 2027. Set against a six-month-high 6.7% jobless rate, a third consecutive fall in employment and WTI at 87.68 and minus 1.00%, a hold is the base case rather than a coin flip, though one month does not kill the hike. Post-print pricing is not yet published; the market voted with the currency, selling the Canadian dollar against all seven others. Gravelle speaks Wednesday 19:30.

CHF.when: December 10 at 10:30, the quarterly assessment, with a hike not expected
CHF.note: The SNB policy rate is 0.00%, unchanged since mid-2025 and held again in September, and previews into December are near-unanimous for another hold. It forecasts average inflation of 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in each of 2027 and 2028. October CPI is 1.5%, close to a three-year high, but core is only 0.5%, so the rise is energy and the bank discounts it. The thing that changed today is not policy but behaviour: in a genuine equity scare the franc was bid, firming against every currency except the yen, which is the opposite of what happened in last week's scare and the reason the franc moves from minus one to zero. TradingEconomics frames it as the franc's renewed haven status eroding carry-trade returns and forcing an unwind. Note the official language has softened, not hardened - the bank removed its prior reference to increased willingness to stem gains in September and officials told lawmakers only that they remain prepared to step in - so December is about the intervention wording rather than the rate.

Net trade took 0.6 percentage points off growth against 0.4 expected, private consumption fell 0.3% and business investment rose 1.6%. catalysts.event: Canada October CPI, median and trimmed CPI (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 15:30, the day's event and the number that decides whether the Bank of Canada's December 9 meeting is live. Headline forecast plus 0.3% m/m from plus 0.1%, median 2.0% from 1.9%, trimmed 1.9% from 1.8%. RBC expects headline to ease to about 3.0% from 3.1% with core slipping to 1.9% and calls a hike its low-conviction base case; Wells Fargo flags upside risk from October oil; the market prices the meeting near 54%. Set against unemployment at a six-month high of 6.7% and WTI down 9.92% on the month. It landed soft: two of the three lines below forecast, headline y/y unchanged at 3.1% where a Reuters poll looked for 3.2%, and the Canadian dollar fell against all seven of the others.

catalysts.event: Fed Chair Warsh speaks on AI and the economy (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 19:00. A red folder on the calendar, but the substance is narrower than the label: this is a Productivity and Jobs Task Force conference in San Francisco on the economic effects of artificial intelligence. Warsh said at the October IMF meetings that he does not believe in saying in advance what he might do at the remaining meetings of the year, and has argued AI could let firms produce more at lower cost. Expect an AI-and-inflation argument rather than a December signal - though with gold already at a 13-month low, anything hawkish extends the metals move. WHAT HE SAID: opening remarks only, with no rates, no December and - against this preview - no inflation at all, even though colleagues have tied the data-centre build-out to price pressure. He set out three staff scenarios, labelled illustrative and not forecasts: broadly shared productivity gains; an expansion with substantial labour-market disruption that pushes unemployment above full employment; and a bust where, after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns turn down and the economy slows. Productivity has been reasonably strong but has not yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside, and the Fed's role is neither advocacy nor opposition. Not market-moving: DXY 103.52 and plus 0.11%, 10-year flat at 5.14%.

At 22:00, three weeks before the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement. Worth reading for any discussion of the housing and credit channel that would bear on how fast the committee is willing to move after October's 4-3 hold.

Delivered at 00:50 on the ASIC Annual Forum State of the Economy panel in Sydney, and she did not sound the pause: wire reports have her keeping the board's current view that inflation risks are still skewed to the upside and flagging the risk of oil prices remaining high, with no new December guidance reported. The RBA has published no transcript - its speeches page still carries only the live broadcast - so the detail of the Q and A is not yet verifiable. The market was unmoved: AUD/USD went on to 0.67318, minus 0.58%, the weakest since late January.

At 02:30, downgraded to a low folder this week but carrying the detail that matters: what the three dissenters argued. If they held because they think the cycle is done rather than on timing, the Aussie has further to fall even from minus two.

At 04:00, previous 2.34%, and the cleanest single read on the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement. The committee held at 2.75% in October only 4-3 against pricing near 90% for a hike, said tighter policy is likely to be required, and carries its own forecast of inflation worsening to about 4.4% in Q4. TradingEconomics and Westpac look for 3.00% in December while ANZ expects a pause. A rise here ends the NZD/USD short; a fall takes the kiwi to zero and unwinds AUD/NZD.

catalysts.event: UK labour market and average earnings
catalysts.note: At 09:00. Average earnings forecast to slow to 3.5% three-month on year from 3.7%, with the unemployment rate at 4.7% and claimant count change forecast plus 28,100. Comes a day before CPI and leans the same way: a cooling wage number makes December 17 harder for the hawks on an MPC that hiked 8-1 on November 5.

catalysts.event: US October retail sales and core retail sales (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 15:30. Headline forecast plus 0.2% after plus 0.8%, core plus 0.4% after plus 0.9%. The first genuine two-way US data risk since the October CPI print on November 10, and the test of whether the consumer can carry the Fed path the whole board is positioned long. December 9 is now roughly 92% to 93.5% priced on CME-based measures, up from 88.8% on November 10, so a bad miss is the first real crack in it. Waller speaks at 16:10 and Hammack at 16:30 the same afternoon.

catalysts.event: Nvidia October-quarter results, after the US close
catalysts.note: The biggest event of the week that no red-folder list carries, and after today it is the single clearest invalidation of four separate theses here: the yen upgrade, the franc upgrade, the silver short and the Aussie short. The reaction lands in Wednesday's Asian and European sessions. Consensus revenue is about 109 billion dollars, with options pricing an earnings-day move near plus or minus 7%. The company's market value has fallen from about 5.8 trillion dollars in early October to 3.9 trillion on Friday, when the stock closed at 162.85 after a 12.75% weekly fall.

At 02:30, forecast plus 0.9% on the quarter after plus 0.8%, with the annual rate last at 3.2%. One of the RBA's stated conditions for inflation persistence. A hot print is the main scheduled thing that could reopen the December 8 hike the market has now largely written off.

At 09:00, forecast 3.6% from 3.5% with core steady at 2.8% and RPI at 4.1%. The week's binary for sterling and the thing that decides whether the only genuinely unpriced December on this board stays live. The MPC hiked to 4.00% on November 5 by 8-1 with Mann dissenting for 50bp and projects CPI rising to around 5% by mid-2027. A print at 3.4% or below makes December 17 much harder and turns GBP/USD into a short.

At 09:30, half an hour after the CPI print, which makes this the most informative half-hour of the week for sterling. Bailey has said another increase may be needed unless inflation risks ease while warning against reading November as the start of a long series of rises.

At 20:00, after Tuesday's inflation expectations print and three weeks before the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement. Breman was one of the four who voted to hold in October against market pricing near 90% for a hike, so his read on whether that was timing or substance matters directly for AUD/NZD.

At 21:00, and the real Fed event of this week rather than Monday's speech. The October 28 meeting held at 3.75% to 4.00% with Governor Cook and Cleveland's Hammack dissenting in favour of a quarter-point rise. What the market needs is the width of the hawkish bloc behind those two: a wide one supports a path now priced at 92% to 93.5% for December, a narrow one is the strongest argument yet against the dollar at plus two.

At 05:30. A hold at 4.85% is now the base case rather than a close call, after the November statement dropped its explicit reference to further increases and three of nine members voted against the hike. This week's three domestic tests - Bullock tonight, the minutes and Thursday's jobs - are what confirm or break that.

At 03:00, a full statement with new forecasts. TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% from 2.75% and Westpac looks for December and February moves to a 3.5% neutral, while ANZ expects a pause - an unusually wide split. Tuesday's Q4 inflation expectations is the direct input.

At 16:45, a regular decision with no Monetary Policy Report, priced near a coin flip at about 54%. Today's CPI decides whether it is live. The bank hiked to 2.50% in October, its first rise in three years, and said there could be a need to go further although caution is necessary.

At 21:00, with a fresh Summary of Economic Projections and dot plot. Roughly 92% to 93.5% priced for a quarter-point on CME-based measures, which would take the range to 4.00% to 4.25%, with a 6.5% to 8% tail for fifty basis points. The projections are where the path the dollar is long gets confirmed or capped.

At 10:30. A hold at 0.00% is near-unanimous in previews. Watch instead for the language on FX intervention, which is what actually caps the franc - and note it has softened rather than hardened, with the bank dropping its reference to increased willingness in September and officials telling lawmakers only that they remain prepared to step in.

catalysts.event: Bank of England Bank Rate decision
catalysts.note: At 14:00, and still genuinely two-sided - the only December outside the US that is not effectively priced. A hike would take Bank Rate to 4.25% from 4.00%. Wednesday's CPI and Bailey's two appearances are what move it.

catalysts.event: ECB rate decision and press conference
catalysts.note: At 15:15, the final meeting of 2026. All 71 economists in the November 10 to 12 Reuters poll expect the deposit rate at 2.75%, but only 46 call it the peak and 25 see another in early 2027 - and the market is more hawkish still, with traders priced for three moves over the next year. New staff projections accompany it.

At 05:00. TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% from 1.25%, a Reuters-poll majority agrees and an October Bloomberg survey had 83% on December - and today's contracting quarter did not change any of that. Nearly three-quarters of a Reuters panel expect another dissent at the next hike to weigh on the yen, which is the detail that matters more than the decision.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz, Iran and US talks
catalysts.note: The weekend escalated and crude did not follow. Iran said it targeted a US radar in Bahrain, the Revolutionary Guards claimed tankers struck mines in the strait and said it remains closed, and the US military disputes the mine claims while Saudi operator Bahri sends tankers through in coordination with it. Diplomacy is reported stalled, with Iran's negotiator saying Tehran wants to move beyond no war, no peace. Transits remain far below pre-conflict levels. Any escalation large enough to actually bid crude gaps USOIL higher and is the clearest invalidation of the gold and silver shorts.

geopolitics: The transmission to watch is a risk premium that has now stopped responding to the news that should create it. Over the weekend Iran said it targeted a US radar installation in Bahrain, the Revolutionary Guards claimed tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and said the waterway remains closed to commercial shipping, and reports had the United States and Israel weighing fresh strikes while Tehran warned of a wider conflict. The US military disputes the mine claims and says the main routes are clear; Saudi operator Bahri is moving oil tankers through in coordination with it. Diplomacy is stalled - Iran's chief negotiator says Tehran wants to move beyond no war, no peace - and the June ceasefire mediated by Pakistan lapsed in August with no deal. That is an escalating weekend by any reading, and crude barely moved: WTI is 88.76 and plus 0.23%, Brent 95.75 and minus 0.10% and down 12.60% on the month, both still up roughly 48% to 49% on the year, which is the premium that remains rather than the premium being added. The read follows directly and it is the same one as Friday, now with a stronger test behind it. A premium that will not bid on an attack on a US facility is a premium being unwound, which is why USOIL stays a range rather than a long and why the Canadian dollar sits at zero rather than plus one: the Bank of Canada hiked in October specifically to stop high energy prices spreading into other goods and services, and energy has fallen about 10% since. But the distribution is not symmetric, and LSEG's point remains the important one - even a diplomatic agreement would not quickly restore normal shipments, because mine clearance, insurance costs and shipowners' willingness to sail all lag any deal. The downside is a bleed and the upside is a gap. What changed today is the franc leg, and it is worth being precise about it. The old regime had a Hormuz escalation bidding oil, gold and the franc together. Last week broke that: a genuine risk event arrived in the form of the AI selloff, the franc was the worst G10 performer and the dollar took the haven bid. Today tested it again with a bigger equity move - the Nikkei down 1.6%, the Kospi 2.8% - and the result split the difference: the franc was bid, modestly, against everything but the yen, while gold fell 0.75% and the dollar index fell 0.02%. So havens are being chosen rather than bought as a group, and the ranking right now is yen first, franc second, dollar and gold not at all. That is a rates-dominant risk-off, and it is why the franc moves to zero while the metals shorts stay on. The European gas leg is the quieter one and still cuts against the DAX: EU gas at 90.14 euros per megawatt hour is up 2.39% on the month and 186.92% on the year, which cancels much of the tailwind that Brent down 12.60% would otherwise give GER40 and keeps euro-area headline inflation at a three-year high of 4.0% while core sits at 2.5% - a hike bought with energy rather than with wages.
